body:
I thought it's correct.
Under `[2, "double"]`, the rule does not check content of strings.

``` js
/*eslint quotes: [2, "double"]*/
var escaped = "a string containing 'single' quotes"; // valid.
var escaped = 'a string containing "double" quotes'; // invalid. it should enclose with double quotes and it should escape double quotes in the string.
```

``` js
/*eslint quotes: [2, "double", "avoid-escape"]*/
var escaped = "a string containing 'single' quotes"; // valid.
var escaped = 'a string containing "double" quotes'; // valid single quotes to avoid escaping double quotes in the string.
```

I'm not sure I understand the rule the same way.  Without `"avoid-escapes"`, I think ALL quotes should follow the rules specified, and nested quotes must be escaped rather than using the alternate style.

Maybe that's just my assumption, that the outer quotes should always follow the rules, and the inner quotes should either be escaped, or the `"avoid-escapes"` option should be used to enable alternate style within.
The option seems to be added in this issue: #199
@IanVS It's slightly different. Without `avoid-escape` this rule will accept escaped quotes as well as another type of quotes inside strings. With it, it will flag any escaped quotes.

This also passes:

``` js
/*eslint quotes: [2, "double", "avoid-escape"]*/

var escaped = 'a string containing \'single" quotes';
```

So, it seems that the only condition when using `"avoid-escape"` is that one of the correct kinds of quotes is found somewhere in the string.  It allows the non-standard quotes to be used on the outermost positions, that's it.

There's currently no way to force the use of escaping to maintain a single style of quotes.  Not sure if that's a bug or not, but it seems like something which should be possible to enforce.
Agree. Latest examples seems like a bug

Just to close the loop: this rule is about quotes used to define strings and nothing else, so no "inner quote" checking is done unless the "avoid-escape" option is used. Even then, it only makes sure that you don't escape a quote character because you used it in the string.

> Even then, it only makes sure that you don't escape a quote character because you used it in the string.

This may be the intent, but as I showed [above](https://github.com/eslint/eslint/issues/3646#issuecomment-137647092), it is not the current behavior.

The current behavior of `"avoid-escape"` is to allow the opposite quote style around a string, as long as the specified quote style is found within the string.
Yes, as @ilyavolodin mentioned, that's a bug. We're in agreement on that.
Actually, looks like a bunch of problems. I'll work on this.
I would prefer avoid-escape to mean that you _may_ avoid escaping internal quotes by changing the delimiter, not that you _must_ do so. If this is changed, my use case will be lost.

Agreed. Looking at the original issue (#199), I believe the correct functionality is to add an exception so that strings pass rather than adding one so that they fail. Example:

``` js
// functionality for quotes: [1, "double"]
var foo = "this is \"my\" string"  // pass
var foo = 'this is "my" string'  // warn

// functionality for quotes: [1, "double", "avoid-escape"]
var foo = "this is \"my\" string"  // pass
var foo = 'this is "my" string'  // pass, because double quotes found inside
```

https://github.com/eslint/eslint/issues/3646#issuecomment-137858218 seems to be the current behavior.

My original question was about:

``` js
// functionality for quotes: [1, "double"]

var foo = "this is 'my' string"  // warn or pass?
```

I'm thinking this should pass based on the above discussion.  If so, this issue can be closed.
@IanVS first example should pass without warning. Second should fail.
